data.title: Lasertec vs SCREEN stock: Tokyo's 27-point split tests profit plans
data.description:
Tokyo's semiconductor-equipment trade split sharply at Monday's close. Lasertec finished November 2 at ¥40,720, up 8.01% from its October 30 close of ¥37,700, while SCREEN Holdings closed at ¥9,218, down 18.96% from ¥11,375. The difference was 26.97 percentage points. These are Tokyo Stock Exchange regular-session closes at 3:30 p.m. Japan time, as recorded by Yahoo Finance's Lasertec and SCREEN historical price feeds, rather than live quotations.

That extraordinary one-day separation poses a more useful question than which stock "won" Monday: which company's published profit plan asks investors to assume the bigger recovery from the results already delivered? TECHi's reconstruction of the two companies' October 30 filings shows a different kind of hurdle for each. Lasertec must generate ¥109.231 billion of operating profit in its remaining three fiscal quarters to meet its unchanged full-year forecast. SCREEN must generate ¥101.977 billion in its second fiscal half. Those figures are simple differences between company guidance and reported profit; they are requirements implied by management targets, not independent forecasts of what either company will earn.

Two closing prices, two different businesses

The share-price comparison is striking, but the firms do not sell interchangeable equipment. Lasertec specializes in inspection and metrology, including tools for advanced photomasks. SCREEN's semiconductor production equipment business is centered on wafer cleaning. Both have exposure to complex chip manufacturing, but the timing of customer orders, equipment delivery, acceptance, service revenue and profit recognition can diverge. An AI spending cycle can help both without moving their quarterly income statements together.

The releases also cover different fiscal calendars. Lasertec reported the first quarter of its year ending June 2027. SCREEN reported the first half of its year ending March 2027. Comparing their quarterly sales as if they covered the same period would be misleading. The meaningful comparison is the profit still needed within each company's own fiscal year, and the amount of execution investors are buying at Monday's closing price.

Neither company attributed Monday's market move to a particular analyst's interpretation. Investors may have reacted to order commentary, the absence of a guidance change, positioning or other factors. The closes establish the divergence; they do not prove its cause. The published filings establish the arithmetic beneath the investment case.

Lasertec: the order story still has to become recognized profit

Lasertec's October 30 quarterly filing reports ¥40.369 billion of sales and ¥15.769 billion of operating profit in the July-to-September quarter. Sales fell 25.5% and operating profit fell 41.0% from the same quarter a year earlier. Its ¥10.734 billion of profit attributable to owners was down 43.7%. The operating margin was 39.06%, calculated as ¥15.769 billion divided by ¥40.369 billion. That is a strong absolute margin, but the profit decline is too large to ignore because the stock rose.

Management maintained its fiscal 2027 forecast of ¥290 billion in sales and ¥125 billion in operating profit. It also described demand tied to AI data centers, CPUs, GPUs and high-bandwidth memory and said its order outlook exceeded prior assumptions. That provides a plausible reason to examine future equipment demand. It does not guarantee that orders become this year's revenue, that acceptance falls inside the remaining quarters, or that production costs remain unchanged.

Subtracting the reported quarter from full-year guidance leaves ¥249.631 billion in sales and ¥109.231 billion in operating profit for the following three quarters. The required average is ¥83.210 billion of quarterly sales and ¥36.410 billion of quarterly operating profit, or roughly 2.06 times and 2.31 times the just-reported first quarter, respectively. The implied operating margin over that remaining stretch is 43.76%. This is TECHi's original profit bridge, not a management forecast for each quarter.

The timing matters. Lasertec's quarterly filing shows equipment sales of ¥23.849 billion, down 42.9% year over year, while service revenue rose 31.2% to ¥16.011 billion. Services can support the business while equipment deliveries are uneven, but the full-year target still requires a much larger flow of recognized sales and profit than the opening quarter delivered. The strongest bull case is that orders and delivery schedules make the first quarter a poor guide to the rest of the year. The strongest bear case is that order strength arrives later than recognition needed for fiscal 2027, or at lower margins than the forecast implies.

One cash-flow detail also deserves care. The company reported ¥39.102 billion of operating cash inflow for the quarter, but the filing says customer advance receipts were a significant driver. Advance cash is encouraging as a sign of customer commitment; it is not the same thing as already earned operating profit. A forecast built from cash alone would overstate what has been delivered on the income statement.

SCREEN: cheaper on guidance, but a steep second-half ramp

SCREEN's October 30 half-year filing shows ¥308.453 billion of sales and ¥54.523 billion of operating profit for the six months through September. Those numbers rose 12.5% and 17.4% year over year. Profit attributable to owners rose 18.2% to ¥37.656 billion. The company kept its full-year forecast at ¥743 billion of sales and ¥156.5 billion of operating profit, figures also displayed on its investor financial highlights page.

The implied remaining-half hurdle is ¥434.547 billion of sales and ¥101.977 billion of operating profit. That means second-half sales must be 1.41 times first-half sales, while second-half operating profit must be 1.87 times first-half profit. SCREEN's first-half operating margin was 17.68%; the unchanged full-year target implies 23.47% for the second half, a 5.79-percentage-point improvement. A low share price relative to guidance therefore comes with a demanding earnings acceleration.

The semiconductor production equipment segment delivered ¥251.398 billion of first-half sales and ¥57.528 billion of operating profit. The filing points to stronger DRAM and post-sales demand but weaker foundry demand, and regional changes that include more U.S. and Korean sales but less Taiwan sales. Those mixed drivers matter more than a generic claim that all AI capital spending lifts every supplier. Memory spending can support cleaning tools; an adverse foundry mix or delayed acceptance can still disrupt the margin bridge.

SCREEN's headline first-half results were positive, yet the stock fell almost a fifth at the next Tokyo close. The selloff may reflect concerns about expectations embedded in the price before the report, the second-half concentration of guidance, the demand mix, or factors outside the filing. The disclosure itself does not identify a single cause. What can be checked is the scale of the remaining profit required: nearly ¥102 billion in six months against ¥54.5 billion already earned in the prior six.

What Monday's prices imply, and what they do not

A simple valuation check makes the contrast sharper. Lasertec's published fiscal 2027 earnings-per-share forecast is ¥1,003.27. Dividing Monday's ¥40,720 close by that company forecast produces 40.59 times guided earnings. SCREEN's corresponding published forecast is ¥607.72 per share after its stated share-split treatment. Its ¥9,218 close divided by that number is 15.17 times guided earnings. The resulting multiple gap is about 2.68 to one.

Those ratios are deliberately narrow. They are price-to-company-guidance figures at one closing snapshot, not forward consensus multiples, target prices or total-return forecasts. The fiscal years end three months apart, and earnings-per-share estimates can change with business results, shares outstanding, taxes and non-operating items. Debt, cash, capital intensity and the durability of each company's earnings also differ. Price-to-earnings alone cannot rank fundamentally different equipment franchises.

The balance sheets make a debt-driven explanation for the entire multiple gap too simple. At September 30, Lasertec reported ¥110.768 billion of cash and cash equivalents. SCREEN reported ¥196.411 billion of cash and cash equivalents against ¥8.406 billion of interest-bearing debt in its own financial highlights; these are absolute amounts for differently sized companies, not comparable cash per share or enterprise-value multiples. Lasertec reported 94.286 million issued shares including treasury stock, while SCREEN reported 190.760 million on its post-split basis. A raw share-price comparison therefore says nothing about relative market capitalization. Enterprise-value comparisons would need synchronized market capitalizations and a consistent treatment of cash, debt and leases, which this closing-price snapshot does not supply.

The comparison still defines a practical decision. Lasertec commands a much higher price per yen of guided earnings, even though its first-quarter operating profit fell sharply. Investors paying that multiple are effectively betting that order strength converts into the larger sales and profit run rate implied by guidance and persists beyond one fiscal year. SCREEN trades at a lower guided multiple, but the discount is not automatically a bargain when the published plan depends on an almost 87% jump in second-half operating profit from the first half.

At Monday's closing snapshot, the price action favored Lasertec's future-order narrative and punished SCREEN's need to execute its unchanged target. That is a description of market pricing, not proof that either thesis is right. A cheaper multiple can stay cheap or fall further if earnings miss. A premium multiple can remain justified if an inspection tool's orders and margins exceed the market's expectations. Neither outcome follows automatically from the one-day gap.

A conditional forecast for the next reports

The next evidence to watch for Lasertec is whether actual recognized equipment sales and operating profit begin to approach the ¥83.210 billion and ¥36.410 billion quarterly averages implied by the unchanged annual plan. A second quarter far below those marks would leave more of the target concentrated in the final half, raising execution risk. A quarter above them, accompanied by clear order-to-revenue timing and stable margins, would make the 40.59-times guided earnings valuation easier to defend. This is a checkpoint, not a prediction that the shares will rise or fall on a particular date.

For SCREEN, the key question is whether second-half production-equipment deliveries and mix can support the required ¥101.977 billion of operating profit at an implied 23.47% margin. Evidence of rising recognized sales and a margin approaching that level would strengthen the case that Monday's steep selloff went too far. More order intake without timely revenue conversion, or a weaker foundry and regional mix, would leave the full-year target exposed. An updated company forecast would supersede this bridge and require the calculation to be rebuilt.

There is an important counterargument to reading too much into either arithmetic test. Equipment businesses can be lumpy: a few high-value deliveries and customer acceptances can make one quarter look abnormally weak and the next unusually strong. The companies' own schedules and customer behavior may support the planned ramps even when a simple average looks imposing. Conversely, neither company's annual guidance is a guaranteed baseline, and Monday's closing prices may have reflected expectations that were never visible in the filings.

The clear conclusion is narrower and more useful than a one-day winner call. Lasertec needs to turn a stronger order outlook into sharply higher reported profit to justify a premium valuation. SCREEN needs a much stronger second half to validate a lower company-guidance multiple. The 26.97-point price split tells investors the market treats those risks very differently. The next releases will show whether the profit bridges, rather than the closing tape, deserve the last word.

data.title: Datadog stock forecast: Q3 explains 95% of the sales upgrade
data.description:
Datadog’s revenue upgrade is less forward-looking than it first appears. Using the midpoints of the company’s forecasts, TECHi calculates that 95% of the $60 million increase in its full-year sales outlook is explained by third-quarter revenue beating its previous guidance. The fourth-quarter outlook leaves revenue roughly flat from the quarter just reported, with a materially lower adjusted operating margin.

That distinction matters for the Datadog stock forecast after a sharp premarket repricing. Yahoo Finance’s timestamped feed recorded DDOG at $183.50 at 7:38:21 a.m. EST on November 4, down 16.8% from the November 3 regular-session close of $220.52. This is a fixed, extended-session observation, not a live quote; the feed’s delay was not specified. The U.S. regular session had not opened.

The third-quarter earnings release, published at 7:01 a.m. EST, reported $1.197 billion of revenue, up 35% year over year. Datadog also introduced its specialized Scout 1.0 model in preview. Strong reported growth and a new AI product, however, do not remove the need to examine how much additional growth the new forecast actually promises.

The 95% calculation behind the upgraded outlook

In its August earnings release, Datadog forecast third-quarter revenue of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion. The midpoint was $1.140 billion. It also projected full-year revenue of $4.45 billion to $4.47 billion, with a $4.460 billion midpoint.

Actual third-quarter sales were $1.197090 billion, according to the financial statements accompanying today’s release. That is $57.09 million above the old quarterly midpoint, or 5.0%. The new full-year range of $4.515 billion to $4.525 billion has a $4.520 billion midpoint, an increase of $60 million.

Divide the $57.09 million quarterly excess by the $60 million annual increase and the result is 95.2%. This is a comparison with Datadog’s own prior forecast, rather than an estimate of the beat against Wall Street consensus. It shows that nearly all the annual sales upgrade can be reconciled to business already delivered in the September quarter.

The calculation does not establish why any investor sold shares. Nor does it mean the company has stopped growing. It identifies the part of the upgrade that offers little fresh evidence about the coming quarter. For investors paying for sustained AI-driven expansion, that distinction is more useful than treating every increase in annual guidance as an equally strong signal.

The fourth-quarter revenue midpoint is $1.195 billion, just below the third quarter’s exact $1.197090 billion. The implied sequential change is approximately minus 0.2%. Guidance can prove conservative, but the published numbers do not currently promise another sequential step up.

A four-point margin reset is the next earnings test

The profit outlook makes the sales arithmetic more consequential. Datadog generated $334.289 million of non-GAAP operating income in the third quarter. Its fourth-quarter forecast is $280 million to $290 million, or $285 million at the midpoint.

That implies a 14.7% sequential decline in adjusted operating income. Dividing each quarter’s operating income by its corresponding revenue gives a third-quarter adjusted margin of 27.9% and a fourth-quarter midpoint margin of 23.8%. The difference is about 4.1 percentage points.

These are TECHi calculations from the company’s reported figures and guidance. They are not management’s forecast for the share price. They also compare an achieved quarter with a future range, so the apparent deterioration can narrow if revenue or spending turns out better than the midpoint assumptions.

For a useful operating sensitivity, suppose fourth-quarter revenue reaches $1.24 billion and the adjusted margin holds at 27%. That would produce approximately $335 million of adjusted operating income, close to the third-quarter result. Conversely, $1.16 billion of sales at a 22% margin would produce about $255 million. Both are illustrative assumptions outside the central guidance case; they show how revenue conversion and expense discipline can change the earnings outcome.

The important question for the next report is therefore not simply whether sales rise year over year. It is whether additional usage, product adoption and customer spending can support profit without requiring an equal increase in the expense base. The DDOG earnings page provides a place to follow the next reported results against these dated expectations.

AI adoption is promising, but the revenue bridge is incomplete

Datadog sells observability and security software that helps customers understand their applications, infrastructure and related systems. More complex AI deployments can create demand for monitoring, troubleshooting and security. That business mechanism gives the company a relevant place in the AI investment discussion without requiring it to manufacture accelerators or own enormous data centers.

The new release says Scout 1.0, Datadog’s first specialized model, powers Bits Investigation in preview. The company claims frontier-model performance at a fraction of the inference cost. That is a company performance claim, not an independently verified benchmark in this article. Preview availability also should not be confused with a disclosed, mature revenue stream.

Datadog reported approximately 4,860 customers with at least $100,000 in annual recurring revenue, compared with about 4,060 a year earlier. That is roughly 20% growth in the large-customer count. Revenue grew faster, at 35%, but those measures describe different populations and time frames. Their difference does not by itself establish average customer spending growth or the contribution from AI customers.

The release does not give a separate revenue number for Scout. Investors therefore cannot responsibly value the product by assigning a published sales multiple to a revenue stream the company has not quantified. Evidence that would strengthen the forecast includes disclosed commercial adoption, repeat usage, identifiable monetization and improved economics after the cost of serving those workloads.

Cash generation and stock compensation tell different parts of the story

There is meaningful operating progress beneath the market reaction. Datadog reported $74.706 million of GAAP operating income, compared with a $5.809 million operating loss a year earlier. Its positive GAAP result gives the growth story more support than adjusted earnings alone would provide.

The gap between GAAP and adjusted operating income still matters. Third-quarter stock-based compensation was $237.181 million. That accounts for approximately 91% of the $259.583 million difference between GAAP and non-GAAP operating income. Other reconciling items include payroll taxes on employee stock transactions, acquired-intangible amortization and acquisition costs.

Stock compensation does not consume cash when recognized in the same way as a salary payment, but it remains relevant to shareholders because equity awards can dilute their ownership. Weighted average diluted shares rose from 362.001 million to 375.014 million year over year, about 3.6%. The two observations should be assessed together rather than treating all non-cash expense as economically irrelevant.

Operating cash flow was $289.951 million. Subtracting $10.872 million of property and equipment purchases and $28.445 million of capitalized software costs produces the company’s $250.634 million free cash flow. That is a 20.9% revenue margin, compared with about 24.2% a year earlier. Free cash flow grew in dollars while its share of revenue declined.

Datadog also held approximately $5.2 billion of cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities. That supports financial flexibility, although it should not be mistaken for wholly surplus equity value: the balance sheet also includes convertible notes and other obligations. The DDOG financials are useful context for comparing cash generation, expenses and balance-sheet capacity across reporting periods.

A conditional Datadog stock forecast for 2027

At the fixed $183.50 premarket observation, the shares traded at approximately 67 times the midpoint of management’s new $2.73–$2.75 full-year non-GAAP earnings-per-share forecast. This is a price-to-adjusted-earnings calculation, not a GAAP P/E. The denominator remains a company estimate, and the price can change substantially during the regular session.

The sensitivity to the valuation multiple is substantial. Holding the $183.50 price at a hypothetical 50 times earnings would require EPS of $3.67, about 34% above the $2.74 guidance midpoint. At 60 times earnings, it would require roughly $3.06, approximately 11.6% growth. These are arithmetic thresholds, not claims about the multiple investors will award.

A wider set of 2027 sensitivities makes the trade-off explicit. Starting with the same $2.74 base, 15% EPS growth and a 50-times multiple imply about $158 per share. Growth of 25% and a 60-times multiple imply about $206. Growth of 35% and a 70-times multiple imply about $259. These are illustrative combinations chosen to show the interaction of growth and valuation; they carry no assigned probabilities and are not company guidance or guaranteed targets.

The downside case can therefore include continuing earnings growth. A smaller multiple can outweigh that growth. The upside case requires both stronger earnings and a valuation that remains demanding in absolute terms. Investors should compare those assumptions with their own required return and with the cost of alternative AI exposures.

The strongest counterargument to a cautious reading is straightforward: Datadog just exceeded its own sales forecast, has growing large-customer adoption and is producing cash. Another conservative guide could leave room for a repeat. The evidence that would change the cautious interpretation is equally clear: a fourth-quarter result that restores sequential growth while defending profitability, followed by a 2027 outlook that converts AI adoption into measurable earnings gains.

Until then, the central forecast test is the bridge between reported success and future profit. The 35% growth headline describes the quarter already completed. The next valuation argument depends on how much of that momentum Datadog can carry into the quarter ahead.

data.title: Rohm lifts profit forecast 67%; depreciation drop matches 85% of H1 gain
data.description:
Rohm raised its annual operating-profit forecast by 66.7% on November 5, citing stronger AI-related server demand and improving profitability. The Japanese semiconductor maker now expects ¥50 billion for the year ending March 2027. But its newly released accounts show why investors should distinguish a recovery in reported profit from growth in earnings before depreciation.

TECHi calculates that the ¥8.389 billion decline in first-half depreciation was equivalent to 85.3% of the ¥9.834 billion increase in operating profit. Rohm’s own simplified EBITDA measure rose just 4.2%, against 128.5% growth in operating profit. That does not erase the genuine revenue recovery; it changes the test for whether the higher forecast represents a durable improvement in the business.

The upgrade is large, even after allowing for the accounting benefit

Rohm’s revised forecast covers April 1, 2026 through March 31, 2027. Expected revenue rises from ¥510 billion to ¥550 billion, an increase of 7.8%. Operating profit rises from ¥30 billion to ¥50 billion, while expected net profit attributable to owners increases from ¥29 billion to ¥45 billion. The revision was released through TDnet at 3:30 p.m. JST on November 5.

The difference between the two outlooks is ¥20 billion of operating profit against ¥40 billion of additional revenue. That 50% ratio is a comparison of forecast revisions, not a disclosed margin on individual products or proof that half of every future sales yen becomes profit. It captures a broader change in expected revenue, pricing, costs and business mix over the same fiscal year.

Rohm says server and storage demand remains strong as generative AI drives data-center investment. It also points to recovering factory-automation demand, resilient electrified-vehicle business, pricing initiatives and cost reductions. Management expects profitability to improve more than originally assumed, despite higher material, energy and logistics costs. The disclosure therefore describes a company-wide recovery with an AI contribution, rather than a business whose entire forecast can be assigned to AI chips.

The annual operating margin implied by the new outlook is 9.1%, compared with 5.9% in the previous plan. That 3.2-percentage-point increase is the practical promise investors need to assess. A larger market opportunity helps, but the forecast also requires Rohm to retain more profit from its sales.

What the 85% depreciation comparison actually measures

The first-half earnings report shows operating profit increasing from ¥7.653 billion to ¥17.487 billion. Depreciation expense in the cash-flow statement fell from ¥27.148 billion to ¥18.759 billion. Subtracting each pair produces the ¥9.834 billion profit increase and the ¥8.389 billion depreciation reduction used in TECHi’s calculation.

Dividing ¥8.389 billion by ¥9.834 billion gives 85.3%. This is an arithmetic bridge between two reported measures. It is not an estimate that 85% of customers’ purchases were artificial, nor does it establish that sales growth, pricing or restructuring had no economic value. It shows that most of the increase in profit after depreciation has a counterpart in a lower depreciation charge.

Rohm explicitly says that reduced depreciation following impairment charges in the previous fiscal year contributed to the first-half profit improvement. An impairment reduces the recorded value of assets; subsequent depreciation can then fall. The earlier write-down and the later expense reduction belong to different reporting periods, so reading only the latest operating-profit growth rate misses part of the story.

The company’s simplified EBITDA, defined as operating profit plus depreciation, was ¥36.247 billion, up 4.2%. Adding the published statement inputs, truncated to millions of yen, gives ¥36.246 billion; the ¥1 million difference reflects reporting precision. That small rounding difference does not change the conclusion: earnings before this expense increased much more slowly than operating profit.

The strongest counterargument is that a lower future cost base can still support shareholder returns. A past impairment does not make today’s reported profit unusable. But a stock forecast built on continued 128.5% operating-profit growth would need evidence beyond an expense reduction that has already occurred. EBITDA is also not cash flow: it excludes working-capital movements and does not fund factories by itself.

Server demand is real, but one major segment still loses money

First-half revenue rose 14.4% to ¥279.483 billion. Within the LSI business, Rohm reports strong server-related product growth alongside gains in automotive and industrial applications. Segment revenue increased 12.8% to ¥128.803 billion, and segment profit rose 35.5% to ¥17.556 billion.

The semiconductor devices business offers a more complicated picture. Revenue increased 20.7% to ¥120.720 billion. Rohm describes firm server demand for silicon-carbide power devices and a large increase in server-related silicon power-device sales. Nevertheless, the segment recorded a ¥4.393 billion loss, compared with a ¥9.809 billion loss a year earlier.

The loss narrowed by ¥5.416 billion, a meaningful improvement. It also means that higher sales have not yet produced profitability across this entire segment. Treating stronger AI infrastructure demand as proof that the silicon-carbide business has completed its turnaround would go beyond the results. Rohm continues to identify improving that business’s profitability as an objective.

Elsewhere, modules revenue fell 4.4% to ¥16.392 billion and segment profit declined 30.0% to ¥1.701 billion. The recovery is uneven. Neither the LSI result nor the semiconductor devices result should be presented as a separate AI revenue total, because the company’s reporting categories include several end markets.

For readers comparing Japanese suppliers, TECHi’s Shibaura forecast analysis examines a different issue: converting a much larger equipment order book into recognized revenue. Rohm’s fresh accounts instead make the relationship between depreciation, operating profit and cash generation central to the investment question.

The cash balance rose while operating cash flow fell

Rohm ended September with ¥477.535 billion of cash and cash equivalents, an increase of ¥48.821 billion from March-end. That provides substantial financial resources, but the cash-flow statement does not show that the increase came entirely from stronger trading.

Operating cash inflow declined to ¥25.546 billion from ¥47.190 billion a year earlier, a fall of 45.9%. The statement records a ¥23.331 billion working-capital outflow from receivables and a ¥17.122 billion inflow from trade payables. Those movements help explain why improved reported earnings did not translate into a similar increase in operating cash generation.

Investment activity provided ¥38.488 billion of net cash, including ¥62.754 billion from sales and redemptions of securities and investment securities. Meanwhile, purchases of property, plant and equipment fell to ¥26.682 billion from ¥81.624 billion.

A narrow cash-after-capex calculation is useful here: operating cash flow minus cash purchases of property, plant and equipment was negative ¥1.136 billion, compared with negative ¥34.434 billion a year earlier. This is TECHi’s explicitly defined calculation, not a company free-cash-flow forecast. It excludes securities transactions, subsidies and other investing items. It shows a much smaller funding gap, helped by sharply lower capital spending, while avoiding the assumption that asset sales are recurring operating income.

The balance sheet also lists ¥100 billion of short-term borrowing, ¥100 billion of long-term borrowing and ¥200 billion of bonds. Subtracting those ¥400 billion of financing balances from cash and cash equivalents leaves ¥77.535 billion. That limited comparison excludes other liabilities and is not a measure of cash available for an immediate distribution.

A stock forecast needs the right earnings denominator

At publication, the fixed price used for valuation is Rohm’s November 5 Tokyo close of ¥3,246 at 3:30 p.m. JST, from Yahoo Finance market data. Tokyo’s regular cash session has ended. The provider’s formal delay is unknown. The close was 6.0% below November 4’s ¥3,455, but its timestamp coincides with the disclosure time, so this daily move is not a clean measurement of the market’s response to the new forecast.

The company’s new annual basic EPS forecast is ¥116.56, compared with ¥75.12 previously. At the fixed closing price, that implies 27.8 times company-guidance earnings, versus 43.2 times using the previous forecast at the same price. These are company estimates for the year ending March 2027, not analyst consensus or a normalized earnings valuation.

If actual EPS were 20% below the new estimate, the multiple at an unchanged share price would rise to 34.8 times. That is a sensitivity, not a prediction of a miss or a share-price target. It illustrates how much the apparent valuation improvement depends on achieving the upgraded earnings denominator.

Share structure adds another limitation. Rohm reported first-half basic EPS of ¥40.36 and diluted EPS of ¥34.42. Those measures should not be interchanged, and the company’s annual basic forecast should not be described as a fully diluted estimate. Nor should the prior fiscal year’s large net loss be used to manufacture a meaningful positive trailing P/E.

What would strengthen or weaken the recovery case

The constructive case rests on more than depreciation. Server-related revenue is expanding, the semiconductor devices loss has narrowed, and the annual operating margin target has increased. Evidence that pricing and cost initiatives lift profitability while operating cash flow improves would make the recovery more convincing.

The weaker case would be revenue growth that leaves the power-device segment loss-making and fails to improve cash conversion. Currency also matters: the revised outlook assumes ¥153 per dollar for the second half. A different exchange-rate outcome, higher input costs or weaker automotive and industrial demand could alter the result. The release does not provide enough information to assign a precise stock-price effect to any one of these risks.

What to watch

Rohm says it plans to publish its earnings presentation and supplementary materials on November 6, followed by its semiannual securities report on November 9. The presentation is the next dated opportunity to assess the profit bridge, server demand and restructuring detail. Until those materials arrive, the useful forecast question is whether stronger demand produces growth in earnings and cash beyond the benefit of lower depreciation.

data.title: CIFR stock forecast: first HPC rent meets a $72M operating loss
data.description:
Cipher Digital reported its first high-performance computing lease revenue on November 2, 2026, but its third-quarter filing also showed a $71.9 million operating loss. The company's results put $5.852 million of data-center rent beside $20.849 million of remaining bitcoin-mining sales. The new business is producing revenue; the question for CIFR stock is how quickly it can become large enough to change the consolidated accounts.

That question became more urgent after U.S. trading opened. Google Finance's CIFR quote showed $6.70 at 9:53:50 a.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 2, about 8% below the prior $7.29 close. This is a dated intraday observation, not a closing price or evidence of a single cause for the decline. The useful forecast is an operating threshold: keeping the rest of the quarter unchanged, how much additional rent would be needed to offset the reported operating loss?

The first HPC rent is real, but the scale is still small

Cipher's quarterly income statement separates the two activities. HPC leasing produced $5.852 million in the three months ended September 30, versus zero a year earlier. Bitcoin mining brought in $20.849 million, down from $71.707 million in the prior-year quarter. Total revenue was $26.701 million, down from $71.707 million. The new rent was 21.9% of current-quarter sales; it has not yet replaced the $50.858 million year-over-year contraction in mining revenue.

The direct-cost line is the promising part of the new segment. Reported HPC lease cost of revenue was $0.726 million, leaving $5.126 million after that line, or 87.6% of HPC rent. This is a calculation from the company's reported amounts, not a disclosed segment operating margin. It excludes company-level compensation, overhead, depreciation, financing and future construction costs. Treating that 87.6% as a permanent mature-project margin would be unjustified; the first delivery is a small, early sample.

The same income statement shows why a high direct margin has not yet resolved the equity question. Compensation and benefits were $38.555 million and general and administrative expense $26.359 million. Depreciation and amortization added $18.821 million. The company reported a $71.915 million GAAP operating loss and negative $10 million of adjusted EBITDA. Those are different measures, but both say the new rent has not yet reached a scale that carries the whole enterprise.

A reproducible threshold for the next phase

Here is the static-cost sensitivity. Divide the $71.915 million quarterly operating loss by the new segment's calculated direct margin of 87.6%. That produces roughly $82.1 million of additional quarterly HPC leasing revenue needed to erase the Q3 operating loss if mining revenue, all other revenue and costs, depreciation, and the direct margin were frozen at Q3 levels. Add the $5.852 million already reported, and the implied quarterly rent level is about $88 million, or roughly 15 times the first quarter's HPC rent. The calculation is an analytical hurdle, not company guidance or a prediction of when breakeven will occur.

That hurdle should be read with two cautions. First, additional data halls will bring project expenses and likely more depreciation, so a constant-cost model can make the path look easier than reality. Second, the mining operation is deliberately shrinking; a further fall in mining gross profit would increase the rent needed to compensate. The reverse could also happen: a lower overhead run rate or higher rent yield could improve the bridge. The next two quarterly statements, not the signed headline value of a lease, will show which forces dominate.

A nearer-term checkpoint is adjusted EBITDA. At Q3's negative $10 million, a simple division by the 87.6% direct margin suggests about $11.4 million of incremental quarterly HPC rent would close that particular gap if every other adjusted-EBITDA component stayed fixed. That is a much smaller threshold than GAAP operating breakeven because depreciation and certain other items sit outside adjusted EBITDA. It does not mean $17.3 million of total quarterly rent would make Cipher profitable or cash-flow positive. Investors should ask management to reconcile each new project contribution to both GAAP and cash outcomes.

Why the reported net profit is a poor shortcut

Readers may see a positive Q3 net income figure and think the transition has already succeeded. The reported reconciliation shows $31.596 million of GAAP net income even though operations lost $71.915 million. A $127.180 million gain from the change in fair value of a warrant liability helped bridge that difference. Such a mark-to-market gain can reverse and does not represent rent collected from a customer. It is part of GAAP earnings, but it is not evidence that the data centers have covered their operating burden.

Interest also matters. Q3 interest expense was $58.994 million, against $32.684 million of interest income. The company issued $850 million of zero-coupon convertible notes due in 2032 and equitized most of a smaller 2030 note balance. The zero coupon limits cash interest on that specific issuance, but the consolidated interest line and project financing still need watching. Nor should a share-price forecast turn a large contracted-rent number into today's equity value without accounting for debt, construction spend and the timing of deliveries.

The $9.1 billion lease is a schedule, not Q4 sales

Cipher said the expanded Barber Lake lease has approximately $9.1 billion of contracted revenue over a 20-year term, including about $5.2 billion added in the amendment. The amendment was disclosed in a September 24 filing; repeating the total today does not make the contract itself a new November 2 signing. Dividing $9.1 billion by 20 yields $455 million per year as a simple lifetime average, or $113.75 million per quarter. That average is not the contractual quarterly payment schedule, a 2027 revenue forecast or near-term free cash flow. Cipher says deliveries are phased to the tenant's compute deployment, and the Q3 HPC revenue came from Black Pearl, a different campus.

The actual progression matters more than the headline total. At Black Pearl, rent began when capacity was delivered, and the company says additional halls there and at Barber Lake are scheduled to come online in phases through year-end. Each energized, accepted hall can change recognized rent. A delayed hall can postpone it. The next report needs to show the number of delivered halls or capacity, recognized HPC rent, project operating expense, and whether new debt or equity was needed to finish delivery. Without those pieces, a large multiyear agreement cannot be converted responsibly into a near-term stock price target.

Power rights and financing decide the 2027 branch

Cipher describes a roughly 5.9-gigawatt development pipeline. That is not the same thing as 5.9 gigawatts of energized, leased data centers. In the November 2 update, it reported conditional ERCOT classifications for 1 gigawatt at Colchis and an additional 1.6 gigawatts of studied load with provisional controllable-load designations. It has also begun lateral natural-gas pipeline development that it says could support up to 2.5 gigawatts of on-site generation. These are development steps with regulatory, construction, fuel-supply and financing conditions, not operating megawatts.

The company also identifies 270 megawatts potentially available in 2027 while it advances tenant discussions and design work. Available capacity is not a signed tenant. A bullish 2027 case requires timely power approvals, contracts, construction and rent commencement at attractive project economics. A base case would show steady rent growth but continued consolidated losses while the portfolio is built. A bearish case would see power or tenant delays combine with construction costs or financing pressure. These are conditional paths, not precise share-price forecasts; the disclosed inputs do not justify an honest dollar target today.

This makes dilution and capital structure part of the same forecast. The Q3 balance sheet lists 415.093 million common shares outstanding at September 30, versus 404.963 million at the end of 2025, a 2.5% increase. It also lists $5.447 billion of long-term borrowings and $0.656 billion of cash and equivalents, alongside $1.719 billion of restricted cash. Restricted cash is not interchangeable with freely available cash. Project-level debt may be supported by future rent, but common shareholders still need a clear bridge from completed campuses to cash after interest, maintenance and reinvestment.

What would change the CIFR forecast

The encouraging evidence is tangible: a first $5.852 million rent line, a low direct-cost line at this early stage and more capacity scheduled for delivery. TECHi’s CIFR quote page and forecast page provide dated market and analyst context, which should be kept separate from this filing-based operating test. The counterargument is equally tangible: mining sales fell 70.9% year over year, Q3 operating loss widened to $71.9 million, and reported net income benefited from a warrant revaluation rather than operating profit. The market's early decline does not settle which side wins over 2027. It signals that investors are demanding proof beyond the size of signed contracts.

For a constructive revision, watch for quarterly HPC rent rising toward the $17.3 million static adjusted-EBITDA hurdle and, over a longer period, for the operating-loss bridge to narrow without an equal jump in debt or shares. Those levels are TECHi sensitivities based on Q3 inputs, not company targets. A flat or falling rent line after promised hall deliveries, higher direct costs, weaker project margins or another delay in firm power access would weaken the thesis. An improving GAAP operating result together with cash generation would matter more than an isolated positive net-income print.

What to watch

The next dated test is Cipher's fourth-quarter 2026 results, expected in the next earnings cycle; the company has not provided a confirmed release date in this November 2 update. Before then, watch for disclosures on year-end data-hall delivery, ERCOT's final treatment of conditional load, and new tenant agreements for the 270 megawatts it identifies for 2027. The practical question for CIFR is whether each new megawatt becomes recognized rent and cash quickly enough to outrun the cost of building it.
